questions.question:
**Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select No Improvement.**

__My favourite novelist in all__ was Charles Dickens, who really left his mark on me.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is option 2) i.e. **My favourite novelist of all**.

 [IMAGE: https://lh4.googleusercontent.com/-_FemLGLa7wmlYgWOlBUXj8sKQYVRdDw4vClW_gaJFONwst58_9u45y8e4Phfc9bVUwoWbE8SJShsiZGHIPNOhbIqSzru_z2aiNDzQlLLpLIfRc04jAR0IwalGmLAMz4YO6s9C4c] __Explanation__:

__
 
• **Let** us **explore** the __**__options__:**

 __
 
• ​The preposition '**in**' is** **used for showing where someone or something is. The prepositional phrase "in all" means in total number; altogether.
 
• The preposition '**of**' is used for concerning or showing someone or something. The prepositional phrase "of all" is used for denoting the least likely or expected.
 
• The preposition '**between**' is used for stating which two people or things are similar or different.
 
• The prepositional phrase "**at** all" (used for emphasis) in any way; to any extent.
 
 
 
• From the context of the sentence, the preposition 'of' should be used in place of 'in'.
 
• Hence, the option "My favourite novelist of all" is correct.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e8d299c1f8ac17c3d0f55c88318dc051a9a17b579eb18127685f8613e4a4990a.png] Extra- Bites-

 
• A **preposition** is a word governing, and usually preceding, a noun or pronoun and expressing a relation to another word or element in the clause.

 

**Correct Sentence__:** ***My favourite novelist of all** was Charles Dickens, who really left his mark on me.*

questions.question:
In the following question, some part of the sentence may have errors. Find out which part of the sentence has an error and select the appropriate option. If a sentence is free from error, select 'No Error'.

The man greeted his secretary and (A)/ told her that he need her help (B)/ to complete the work immediately. (C)/ No error (D)
questions.solution:
The correct answer is option 2) i.e. B

 [IMAGE: https://lh4.googleusercontent.com/-_FemLGLa7wmlYgWOlBUXj8sKQYVRdDw4vClW_gaJFONwst58_9u45y8e4Phfc9bVUwoWbE8SJShsiZGHIPNOhbIqSzru_z2aiNDzQlLLpLIfRc04jAR0IwalGmLAMz4YO6s9C4c] __Explanation__:

__
 
• The given sentence is an **indirect speech** and it is in the simple past tense.
 
• The verb 'need' used in the reported speech is in simple present tense and should be changed to the simple past tense.
 
• The past simple tense format of indirect speech is "**Subject + V2 + Object**".
 
• Thus, the verb 'need' should be converted into 'needed'.
 
• **Hence**, the option "**he need her help**" is erroneous.
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/3c70b9ffb82c473880d52a797d68ed115c96a6b7f44ce381a50aeb5753c1d17b.png] 

 
• If the first part of the sentence (reporting verb part) belongs to the past tense, the tense of reported speech will change. If the first part of the sentence (reporting verb part) belongs to the present or future tense, the tense of reported speech will not change.
 
• The following table will enable us to know how tense changes into Indirect speech:
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 Direct Speech
 Indirect Speech
 
 

 Present simple (Subject +V1st + Object)
 Past simple (Subject +V2 + Object)
 
 

 Present continuous (Subject +is/am/are+V1 +ing+ Object)
 Past Continuous (Subject +was/were+V1 +ing+ Object)
 
 

 Present perfect (Subject + has/have+V3+Object)
 Past perfect (Subject+had+V3+Object)
 
 

 Past simple (Subject+V2+Object)
 Past perfect (Subject+had+V3+Object)
 
 

 Past Continuous (Subject +was/were+V1 +ing+ Object)
 Past perfect continuous (Subject +had been+V1 +ing+ Object)
 
 

 Future simple (Subject+ will/shall+V1+object)
 Present Conditional (Subject+ would+V1+object)
 
 

 Future Continuous (Subject +will/shall+be+V1 +ing+ Object)
 Conditional Continuous (Subject +would+be+V1 +ing+ Object)
 
 
 
 

 

**Correct Sentence__:** *The man greeted his secretary and told her that **he needed her help **to complete the work immediately.*

questions.question:
In the following question, out of the four alternatives, select the alternative which will improve the underlined part of the sentence. In case no improvement is needed, select “No improvement”

Meeting my teacher after ten years was __an unforgotten moment__
questions.solution:
The correct answer is option 2) i.e. an unforgettable moment.

 [IMAGE: https://lh4.googleusercontent.com/-_FemLGLa7wmlYgWOlBUXj8sKQYVRdDw4vClW_gaJFONwst58_9u45y8e4Phfc9bVUwoWbE8SJShsiZGHIPNOhbIqSzru_z2aiNDzQlLLpLIfRc04jAR0IwalGmLAMz4YO6s9C4c] __Explanation__:

__
 
• **Context of the Sentence__:** It's impossible to forget the moment of meeting my teacher after ten years.
 
• The word 'unforgotten' in the sentence is not correct as it means not forgotten (negative adjective).
 
• From the context of the sentence, the correct form of the adjective should be 'unforgettable'.
 
• The adjective 'unforgettable' means something that is so memorable that it can never be forgotten.
 
• Hence, the option "an unforgettable moment" is correct.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/87c1a28e731fadd9279228c1cea2f8e988a3f790bf9ccc89c9b0f02c423b1609.png] 

__
 
• An experience that had a strong effect on you (either good or bad) can be described as unforgettable. 
 
• If you describe something as unforgettable, you mean that it is, for example, extremely beautiful, enjoyable, or unusual, so that you remember it for a long time. You can also refer to extremely unpleasant things as unforgettable.

 

Correct Sentence__: *Meeting my teacher after ten years was **an unforgettable moment***.

questions.question:
**Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.**

In the United States of America two dozen people_______due to the present cold wave.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is option 1) i.e. **have been killed**.

 [IMAGE: https://lh4.googleusercontent.com/-_FemLGLa7wmlYgWOlBUXj8sKQYVRdDw4vClW_gaJFONwst58_9u45y8e4Phfc9bVUwoWbE8SJShsiZGHIPNOhbIqSzru_z2aiNDzQlLLpLIfRc04jAR0IwalGmLAMz4YO6s9C4c] __Explanation__: 

__
 
• The given sentence is a present perfect passive voice. The present perfect is a verb tense which is used to show that an action has taken place once or many times before now. The present perfect is most frequently used to talk about experiences or changes that have taken place.
 
• **Let** us **explore** the given **options**__**:**
 __
 
• "**Have been killed**" is the passive voice for present perfect tense. 'Have' is used with a plural noun.
 
• "**Are being killed**" is the passive voice for present continuous tense.
 
• "**Has killed**" is the active voice for present perfect tense.
 
• "**Has been killed**" is the passive voice for present perfect tense. 'Has' is used with a singular noun.
 
 
 
• In the given sentence "two dozen people" is a plural noun so the plural form of the verb should be used.
 
• Hence, the correct option is "have been killed".

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/87c1a28e731fadd9279228c1cea2f8e988a3f790bf9ccc89c9b0f02c423b1609.png] 

 
• Verbs of passive format have a different set of tenses (*V3 - Past participle or Third form of the Verb) as given below in the table:
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 TENSE
 ACTIVE
 PASSIVE
 PASSIVE CONVERSION
 
 

 Present Simple
 He plays football
 am/is/are + V3
 Football is played by him
 
 

 Present Continuous
 He is playing football
 am/is/are + being +V3
 Football is being played by him
 
 

 Present Perfect
 He has played football
 Has/have + been+ V3
 Football has been played by him
 
 

 Present Perfect Continuous
 He has been playing football
 Not used and unusual.
 Not used and unusual
 
 

 Past Simple
 He played football
 Was/were + V3
 Football was played by him
 
 

 Past Continuous
 He was playing football
 Was/were + being + V3
 Football was being played by him
 
 

 Past Perfect
 He had played football
 Had + been + V3
 Football had been played by him
 
 

 Past Perfect Continuous
 He had been playing football
 Not used and unusual
 Not used and unusual
 
 

 Future Simple
 He will play football
 Will + be + V3
 Football will be played by him
 
 

 Future Continuous
 He will be playing football
 Not used and unusual
 Not used and unusual
 
 

 Future Perfect
 He will have played football
 Will have been + V3
 Football will have been played by him
 
 

 Future Perfect Continuous
 He will have been playing football
 Not used and unusual
 Not used and unusual
 
 
 
 

**Correct Sentence__:** *In the United States of America two dozen people **have been killed** due to the present cold wave*.

questions.question:
**Select the most appropriate option to substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select No Improvement.**

When you go by rail, __make sure taking__ the express train that stops only at big stations.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is option 3) i.e. **make sure to take**.

 [IMAGE: https://lh4.googleusercontent.com/-_FemLGLa7wmlYgWOlBUXj8sKQYVRdDw4vClW_gaJFONwst58_9u45y8e4Phfc9bVUwoWbE8SJShsiZGHIPNOhbIqSzru_z2aiNDzQlLLpLIfRc04jAR0IwalGmLAMz4YO6s9C4c] __Explanation__: 

__
 
• In the given sentence, the form of the verb 'taking' is not correct.
 
• The ‘to-infinitive’ is used in many sentence constructions, often expressing the purpose of something or someone's opinion about something.
 
• Use of infinitive ‘to’ = ‘to’ + base form of the verb (here take).
 
• The ‘infinitive’ is the base form of a verb. 
 
• Thus, the infinitive 'to take' should be used instead of the gerund 'taking'.
 
• Hence, the correct option is "make sure to take".

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e8d299c1f8ac17c3d0f55c88318dc051a9a17b579eb18127685f8613e4a4990a.png] Extra- Bites-

 
• When we talk about the infinitive we are usually referring to the present infinitive, which is the most common. There are, however, four other forms of the infinitive: the perfect infinitive, the perfect continuous infinitive, the continuous infinitive, & the passive infinitive.
 

​Correct Sentence__: *When you go by rail, **make sure to take** the express train that stops only at big stations.*

questions.question:
**From the given options, identify the segment in the sentence which contains the grammatical error.**

After finishing his tiring game, Rohan leaned by the wall.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is option 4) i.e. **by the wall**.

 [IMAGE: https://lh4.googleusercontent.com/-_FemLGLa7wmlYgWOlBUXj8sKQYVRdDw4vClW_gaJFONwst58_9u45y8e4Phfc9bVUwoWbE8SJShsiZGHIPNOhbIqSzru_z2aiNDzQlLLpLIfRc04jAR0IwalGmLAMz4YO6s9C4c] __Explanation__: 

__
 
• In the given sentence, the use of the preposition 'by' is not correct.
 
• The preposition 'by' is used when there is an object you are referencing in relation to a location and you want to indicate nearness or closeness.
 
• The preposition 'on' is used when talking about a defined area (either small or large), but not a specific point; when using ‘on’ the item remains visible and above the surface.
 
• Thus, the preposition 'by' should be replaced by 'on' or 'against'
 
• Hence, the correct option is "by the wall".

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/e8d299c1f8ac17c3d0f55c88318dc051a9a17b579eb18127685f8613e4a4990a.png] Extra- Bites-

 
• "**Lean on**" is a **phrasal verb** that means to depend on someone or something for help and support. If you lean on someone or lean upon them, you depend on them for support and encouragement.

 

Correct Sentence__: *After finishing his tiring game, Rohan leaned **on** **the wall***. OR *After finishing his tiring game, Rohan leaned **against the wall**.*

questions.question:

To have the gift of the gab
questions.solution:
The correct answer is option 1) i.e. To be eloquent.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**:- 

__
 
• Given Idiom__: *To have the gift of the gab* means the ability to speak to others in a self-assured, persuasive manner.

 __
 
• Example: *And when a politician says a mouthful with some degree of articulation, he is said to have the gift of gab.*
 
 
 
• Let us explore the given options__:
 __
 
• To be eloquent means to be fluent or persuasive in speaking or writing.
 
• To be intelligent means having or showing intelligence, especially of a high level.
 
• To be boastful means showing excessive pride and self-satisfaction in one's achievements, possessions, or abilities. 
 
• To be gifted means having exceptional talent or natural ability.
 
 
 
• Hence, the option "To be eloquent" is correct.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• This idiom originates from the Middle English word ‘gob’ which means 'mouth' and ‘gabbe’ which means "idle talk".

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/2f1d776c4ca45212685ca0930c2539d73a1d70923a3eebad6480bea0298a95b3.png] 

 
• दिया हुआ मुहावरा__ :To have the gift of the gab का अर्थ है दूसरों से आत्म-आश्वासन, प्रेरक तरीके से बात करने की क्षमता।

 __
 
• उदाहरण: *And when a politician says a mouthful with some degree of articulation, he is said to have the gift of gab.*
 
 
 
• आइए दिए गए विकल्पों का पता लगाएं__ :
 __
 
• To be eloquent का अर्थ है बोलने या लिखने में धाराप्रवाह या प्रेरक होना।
 
• To be intelligent का अर्थ है बुद्धि होना या दिखाना, विशेष रूप से उच्च स्तर का।

• To be gifted का अर्थ है असाधारण प्रतिभा या प्राकृतिक क्षमता होना।
 
 
 
• इसलिए , विकल्प "to be eloquent" सही है।

questions.question:
**From the given options, identify the segment in the sentence which contains the grammatical error.**

If it weren’t for the old man, we haven’t had anything to talk about.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is option 1) i.e. **we haven’t had**.

 [IMAGE: https://lh4.googleusercontent.com/-_FemLGLa7wmlYgWOlBUXj8sKQYVRdDw4vClW_gaJFONwst58_9u45y8e4Phfc9bVUwoWbE8SJShsiZGHIPNOhbIqSzru_z2aiNDzQlLLpLIfRc04jAR0IwalGmLAMz4YO6s9C4c] __Explanation__: 

__
 
• The given sentence is a second conditional sentence.
 
• The second conditional is used to refer to a time that is now or any time, and a situation that is unreal. These sentences are not based on fact.
 
• The second conditional is used to refer to a hypothetical condition and its probable result.
 
• In the second conditional sentences, the if clause uses the simple past, and the main clause uses the present conditional or present continuous conditional.
 
• We use the simple past tense in the if-clause and present conditional or present continuous conditional tense in the main clause.
 
• Thus, the correct form of the verb in the main clause here should be "**would + not + be + present participle**".
 
• Hence, the correct option is "we haven’t had".

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• Conditional sentences consist of a main clause and a conditional clause (sometimes called an if-clause). The conditional clause usually begins with if or unless. The conditional clause can come before or after the main clause.
 
• There are four main kinds of conditionals:
 
 
• The Zero Conditional: (if + present simple, ... present simple).
 
• The First Conditional: (if + present simple, ... will + infinitive).
 
• The Second Conditional: (if + past simple, ... would + infinitive).
 
• The Third Conditional. (if + past perfect, ... would + have + past participle).
 
 
 

Correct Sentence__: *If it weren’t for the old man, we **wouldn't be having **anything to talk about.*
